purpose: Define how to hold dying-person and bedside utterances without turning them into prophecy, diagnosis, sentimental last-words mythology, or mandatory scripts.
primary_rule: The utterance is not the record by itself. The record is the whole witnessed moment: exact words when consented, speaker, listener, phase, setting, source, uncertainty, response, interpretation boundaries, and review state.

utterance_source_types.public_use: only with explicit quotation permission and de-identification review
may be summarized but should not be presented as exact words
quarantined until source diversity and review
not public evidence; only a research prompt
must be framed as optional response language, not instruction

required_boundaries: separate exact words from witness interpretation
separate dying-person speech from family/practitioner response language
never infer exact time to death from a phrase
never decide spiritual meaning for the reader
never pressure reconciliation, forgiveness, goodbye, or permission language
index silence and nonresponse with the same seriousness as quotable speech
minimum_fields_for_future_contributed_ut: speaker role and relationship if ethical
whether words are exact, approximate, translated, or paraphrased
who heard them and how soon after death they were recorded
known cognition/delirium/medication caveats only when ethically and clinically reviewed
what meanings were offered by whom
what meanings must not be inferred
blocked_public_patterns: These are the words everyone says before dying.
If they say this, death will happen within X.
You must say this before they die.
This proves they saw the afterlife.
They waited for you or died because you left.
